11 — Example

Full, annotated implementation. Read it after kata submit 11 passes.

The compilable files are reference/ch11/agent/mcp.go and reference/ch11/agent/cmd/agent/main.go. The loop, the prompt and the registry are unchanged.

The shape

mcp.go      StartMCP, call, Initialize, ListTools, CallTool, mcpTool
main.go     spawn, handshake, merge tools, warn and continue on failure

Step 1 — a process, and two pipes

cmd := exec.CommandContext(ctx, "sh", "-c", command)
stdin, _ := cmd.StdinPipe()
stdout, _ := cmd.StdoutPipe()
cmd.Start()

sh -c lets the flag carry arguments, which is how people actually write these commands (npx -y some-server). The server's stderr is not attached: stdout is the protocol, and mixing diagnostics into it breaks the framing on the first warning.

Step 2 — one request, one matching response

func (c *MCPClient) call(ctx context.Context, method string, params any) (json.RawMessage, error) {
	id := nextMCPID()
	// ... write {"jsonrpc":"2.0","id":id,"method":method,"params":params}\n

	for {
		line, err := c.stdout.ReadBytes('\n')
		if err != nil {
			return nil, err
		}
		var resp mcpResponse
		if json.Unmarshal(line, &resp) != nil {
			continue
		}
		if resp.ID == nil || *resp.ID != id {
			continue   // a notification, or an answer to an abandoned request
		}
		if resp.Error != nil {
			return nil, fmt.Errorf("mcp %s: %s (%d)", method, resp.Error.Message, resp.Error.Code)
		}
		return resp.Result, nil
	}
}

The continue on a mismatched id is the line that makes this robust. Servers send notifications for progress and logging, and a client that assumes "the next line is my answer" deadlocks the first time one arrives.

The read runs in a goroutine so ctx can interrupt it. A timed-out request leaves the connection unusable; the chapter says so instead of pretending otherwise.

Step 3 — the handshake, including the silent part

result, err := c.call(ctx, "initialize", map[string]any{
	"protocolVersion": MCPProtocolVersion,
	"capabilities":    map[string]any{},
	"clientInfo":      map[string]any{"name": "kata-agent", "version": "1.0"},
})
// ... record serverInfo.name ...

return c.notify("notifications/initialized", nil)

The notification is the part people skip, because nothing visibly fails when you do: a lenient server answers tools/list anyway. A strict one does not, and the failure looks like a hang.

The server name is taken from the response rather than the command line, because the name in the command is often npx or a path.

Step 4 — namespacing is derived, not hardcoded

func (t *mcpTool) Name() string { return t.server + "." + t.info.Name }

t.server comes from sanitizeName(init.ServerInfo.Name), which lowercases and replaces anything outside [a-z0-9-]. Nothing is hardcoded to demo, so two servers that both expose read produce alpha.read and beta.read.

Without the prefix, read from the server replaces the built-in read, and the model's "I read the file" refers to a file on another machine.

Step 5 — content is a list

var parts []string
for _, block := range call.Content {
	if block.Type == "text" && block.Text != "" {
		parts = append(parts, block.Text)
	}
}
text := strings.Join(parts, "\n")

Two decisions:

  • join, do not take the first. A server that answers with a summary and a detail

block expects both to arrive.

  • filter by type. An image block is base64. Passing it through spends context on

something the model cannot use.

call.IsError is honoured by returning an error, which the registry turns into an IsError result. That distinction matters: a tool that ran and failed is not the same as a transport that broke, but both end up as readable text for the model.

Step 6 — startup failure is a warning

client, err := agent.StartMCP(ctx, *mcpCommand)
if err != nil {
	fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "agent: mcp unavailable: %v\n", err)
} else {
	defer client.Close()
	if err := client.Initialize(ctx); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "agent: mcp handshake failed: %v\n", err)
	} else if err := client.ListTools(ctx); err != nil {
		fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "agent: mcp tools/list failed: %v\n", err)
	} else {
		allTools = append(allTools, client.Tools()...)
	}
}

The nesting is deliberate: each step can fail without taking the run with it, and the agent degrades to its built-in tools. The exit code stays 0, because the person's question was answered.

The child registry is built from baseTools only, so a subagent does not inherit MCP tools. That keeps the child's schema list small and keeps the dependency order simple.

The diffs

1. Skipping the initialized notification — mcp-initialize-handshake

  c.call(ctx, "initialize", ...)
+ c.notify("notifications/initialized", nil)
  c.call(ctx, "tools/list", nil)

2. Using the server's tool name unchanged — mcp-name-collision

- func (t *mcpTool) Name() string { return t.info.Name }
+ func (t *mcpTool) Name() string { return t.server + "." + t.info.Name }

3. Taking only the first content block — mcp-content-blocks-joined

- return call.Content[0].Text, nil
+ // join every text block

4. Exiting when the server is missing — mcp-unavailable-is-survivable

- if err != nil { return 1, err }
+ fmt.Fprintf(os.Stderr, "agent: mcp unavailable: %v\n", err)

internal/fake/mcpserver/main.go150the other side of the protocol

Comparison checklist

  • [ ] server spawned with sh -c, stdout reserved for the protocol
  • [ ] requests carry an id, notifications do not
  • [ ] responses with a foreign id are skipped
  • [ ] initialize then notifications/initialized then tools/list
  • [ ] server name taken from the response and sanitised
  • [ ] tool names namespaced, built-ins untouched
  • [ ] text blocks joined, other types ignored
  • [ ] JSON-RPC error becomes a Go error, then an IsError result
  • [ ] startup failure warns and continues
  • [ ] no tools/call when the model asked for nothing

Differences outside this list are style.
